System.out.println(minutes + " minutes");
System.out.println(seconds + " seconds");

Output:

2 minutes
25 seconds

Integer division determines the complete minutes, while % determines what remains.

docs.title: 13. Numeric Literals
docs.text:
A literal is a value written directly in source code.

int count = 25;
double price = 12.75;
long population = 9000000000L;
float rate = 3.5F;

Examples of integer literals:

10
250
1000000

Examples of floating-point literals:

5.0
12.75
0.125

A floating-point literal is treated as a double by default.

Use F or f for a float:

float value = 10.5F;

Use L or l for a long literal when needed. Uppercase L is easier to distinguish from the digit 1.

long value = 5000000000L;

docs.title: 14. Scientific Notation
docs.text:
Java supports scientific notation for floating-point values.

double largeValue = 1.25e6;
double smallValue = 3.5e-4;

These represent:

1.25 × 10^6
3.5 × 10^-4

Both uppercase E and lowercase e may be used.

docs.title: 15. Floating-Point Precision
docs.text:
Floating-point values are approximations in computer memory. Some decimal calculations may therefore produce results with small precision differences.

For example:

System.out.println(1.0 - 0.9);

The displayed result may not be represented internally as exactly 0.1.

This is an important consideration when working with decimal calculations.

docs.title: 16. Exponent Operations
docs.text:
Java provides Math.pow() for exponentiation.

General form:

Math.pow(base, exponent)

Examples:

System.out.println(Math.pow(3, 2));
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 5));
System.out.println(Math.pow(9, 0.5));

Math.pow() returns a double.

Example:

double side = 4.0;
double squareArea = Math.pow(side, 2);

System.out.println(squareArea);

docs.title: 17. Arithmetic Expressions
docs.text:
Java expressions follow standard arithmetic precedence.

For example:

double result = 5 + 3 * 4;

Multiplication occurs before addition, so the result is:

17

Parentheses can change the order:

double result = (5 + 3) * 4;

Now the result is:

32

Use parentheses when they improve clarity, even when they are not strictly required.

docs.title: 18. Temperature Conversion Example
docs.text:
A practical program can combine input, arithmetic expressions, and output.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class TemperatureConverter {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter Fahrenheit temperature: ");
        double fahrenheit = input.nextDouble();

        double celsius = (fahrenheit - 32) * 5.0 / 9.0;

        System.out.println("Celsius: " + celsius);
    }
}

Notice the use of 5.0 and 9.0 to ensure floating-point division.

docs.title: 19. Augmented Assignment Operators
docs.text:
An augmented assignment operator combines an arithmetic operation with assignment.

Instead of:

score = score + 5;

you can write:

score += 5;

Common forms:

Operator Example Equivalent += x += 5 x = x + 5 -= x -= 5 x = x - 5 *= x *= 5 x = x * 5 /= x /= 5 x = x / 5 %= x %= 5 x = x % 5

These operators make simple updates more concise.

docs.title: 20. Increment and Decrement Operators
docs.text:
Java provides shorthand operators for increasing or decreasing a variable by one.

count++;
count--;

These are equivalent to:

count = count + 1;
count = count - 1;

Java also provides prefix forms:

++count;
--count;

When used by themselves as statements, the prefix and postfix forms have the same final effect on the variable.

When used inside a larger expression, their behavior differs.

docs.title: Postincrement
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = x++;

After execution:

y = 5
x = 6

docs.title: Preincrement
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = ++x;

After execution:

x = 6
y = 6

Avoid overly complicated expressions involving several increment or decrement operations. Clear code is usually preferable to shorter code.

docs.title: 21. Numeric Type Conversion
docs.text:
Java sometimes converts numeric values automatically.

For example:

int count = 10;
double result = count;

The integer value can be widened to a double.

When an expression contains different numeric types, Java promotes values as needed for the calculation.

For example:

int quantity = 4;
double price = 2.5;

double total = quantity * price;

The result is a double.

docs.title: 22. Explicit Type Casting
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to explicitly convert a value.

General form:

(type) value

Example:

double value = 9.8;
int wholeNumber = (int) value;

After the cast:

wholeNumber = 9

The fractional portion is truncated, not rounded.

Another example:

int total = 7;
int count = 2;

double average = (double) total / count;

Casting total to double causes floating-point division.

docs.title: 23. A Simple Program Development Process
docs.text:
Before writing code, identify what the program needs to accomplish.

A useful workflow is:

Requirements
    ↓
Analyze the problem
    ↓
Identify input, process, and output
    ↓
Design the solution
    ↓
Implement the program
    ↓
Test the program
    ↓
Improve and maintain the program

For small introductory programs, the Input-Process-Output model is especially useful.

docs.title: Example: Trip Cost
docs.text:
Input

distance
fuel efficiency
fuel price

Process

gallonsNeeded = distance / fuelEfficiency
tripCost = gallonsNeeded * fuelPrice

Output

tripCost

This planning can be completed before writing Java code.

docs.title: Using a Variable Before It Has a Value
docs.text:
double total;
System.out.println(total);

A local variable must be initialized before it is used.

docs.title: Integer Overflow
docs.text:
Numeric types have finite ranges. A calculation that exceeds the range of an integer type can produce an unexpected value.

Choose a type appropriate for the expected data.

docs.title: Floating-Point Round-Off
docs.text:
Decimal values may not always be represented exactly.

Do not assume every floating-point calculation will produce an exact decimal representation.

docs.title: Unintended Integer Division
docs.text:
int score1 = 7;
int score2 = 8;

double average = (score1 + score2) / 2;

The division is performed using integers before the result is assigned to double.

A better expression is:

double average = (score1 + score2) / 2.0;

docs.title: Creating Unnecessary Scanner Objects
docs.text:
A program normally needs only one Scanner object for reading from System.in.

Prefer:

Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

int age = input.nextInt();
double salary = input.nextDouble();

rather than creating a new Scanner for every input value.

docs.title: 25. Putting the Concepts Together
docs.text:
The following program combines several elementary programming concepts.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class FuelCostCalculator {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter trip distance in miles: ");
        double distance = input.nextDouble();

        System.out.print("Enter vehicle miles per gallon: ");
        double milesPerGallon = input.nextDouble();

        System.out.print("Enter fuel price per gallon: ");
        double pricePerGallon = input.nextDouble();

        double gallonsNeeded = distance / milesPerGallon;
        double totalCost = gallonsNeeded * pricePerGallon;

        System.out.println("Estimated gallons needed: " + gallonsNeeded);
        System.out.println("Estimated fuel cost: $" + totalCost);
    }
}

This program demonstrates:

  • Variables
  • double values
  • Console input
  • Arithmetic expressions
  • Assignment
  • Input-process-output design
  • Console output

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between declaring and initializing a variable?
  2. Why should variable names be meaningful?
  3. What is the purpose of the final keyword?
  4. What is the difference between int and double?
  5. What does Scanner allow a Java program to do?
  6. What is the result of 11 / 4 when both values are integers?
  7. What is the result of 11 % 4?
  8. Why would you use Math.pow()?
  9. What is the difference between x++ and ++x when they appear inside a larger expression?
  10. What happens when a double is explicitly cast to an int?
  11. Why can floating-point calculations sometimes display unexpected decimal digits?
  12. What are the three parts of the Input-Process-Output model?
  13. Why can a program compile successfully and still produce an incorrect numeric result?

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Many programming tasks require the same operation to be performed repeatedly. Writing the same statement many times is inefficient and difficult to maintain. Loops allow a program to repeat a block of code while a condition remains true or for a specified number of iterations.

Java provides three primary loop structures:

  • while
  • do-while
  • for

Although these loop structures can often solve the same problems, each is especially useful in particular situations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this material, you should be able to:

  • Explain why loops are useful in programming.
  • Design and trace a while loop.
  • Identify initialization, continuation condition, loop body, and update operations.
  • Develop counter-controlled and condition-controlled loops.
  • Use sentinel values when the number of inputs is unknown.
  • Write do-while loops when the body must execute at least once.
  • Write for loops for controlled repetition.
  • Select an appropriate loop structure for a programming problem.
  • Create nested loops.
  • Use accumulators and counters to process repeated data.
  • Avoid common infinite-loop and off-by-one errors.
  • Reduce problems caused by floating-point values in loop control.
  • Use break and continue appropriately.
  • Apply loops to computational problems such as greatest common divisor, growth calculations, number conversion, palindrome checking, and prime-number generation.

docs.title: 1. Why Use Loops?
docs.text:
Suppose a program must display the same message 100 times.

Without a loop, the program would require many repeated statements:

System.out.println("Learning Java");
System.out.println("Learning Java");
System.out.println("Learning Java");
// many more...

A loop expresses the repetition directly:

int count = 0;

while (count < 100) {
    System.out.println("Learning Java");
    count++;
}

This version is shorter, easier to modify, and clearly communicates that the operation is repetitive.

docs.title: 2. The Basic Loop Design
docs.text:
A typical loop contains four important components:

  1. Initialization --- establishes the starting state.
  2. Continuation condition --- determines whether another iteration should execute.
  3. Loop body --- contains the statements that repeat.
  4. Update --- changes a value so that the loop eventually reaches its stopping condition.

Example:

int count = 1;              // Initialization

while (count <= 5) {        // Continuation condition
    System.out.println(count); // Loop body
    count++;                // Update
}

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

An iteration is one execution of the loop body.

docs.title: 3. The while Loop
docs.text:
General form:

while (condition) {
    // Statements
}

Java evaluates the condition before executing the body.

If the condition is true, the body executes. Java then returns to the condition and tests it again. When the condition becomes false, the loop terminates.

Example:

int number = 1;

while (number <= 5) {
    System.out.println(number);
    number++;
}

Because the condition is checked first, a while loop can execute zero times.

int number = 10;

while (number < 5) {
    System.out.println(number);
}

The body never executes because number < 5 is false initially.

docs.title: 4. Tracing a while Loop
docs.text:
Consider:

int count = 0;

while (count < 3) {
    System.out.println("Java");
    count++;
}

Trace:

Iteration count Before Test count < 3 Action

1 0 true Print and increment 2 1 true Print and increment 3 2 true Print and increment --- 3 false Exit loop

Output:

Java
Java
Java

Tracing is an effective technique for understanding and debugging loop behavior.

docs.title: 5. Counter-Controlled Loops
docs.text:
A counter-controlled loop executes a known number of times.

Example:

int count = 1;

while (count <= 10) {
    System.out.println("Iteration " + count);
    count++;
}

The variable count acts as the loop counter.

A counter usually requires:

starting value
stopping condition
increment or decrement

Changing any of these can change the number of iterations.

docs.title: 6. Accumulators
docs.text:
An accumulator stores a running result as a loop executes.

Example: sum the integers from 1 through 5.

int number = 1;
int sum = 0;

while (number <= 5) {
    sum += number;
    number++;
}

System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);

Output:

Sum: 15

Here:

  • number is the counter.
  • sum is the accumulator.

Counters and accumulators are frequently used together.

docs.title: 7. Repeating Until a Condition Is Satisfied
docs.text:
The number of iterations is not always known in advance.

Suppose a program asks the user to solve a problem until the answer is correct.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class RepeatUntilCorrect {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        int answer = -1;

        while (answer != 12) {
            System.out.print("What is 7 + 5? ");
            answer = input.nextInt();

            if (answer != 12) {
                System.out.println("Try again.");
            }
        }

        System.out.println("Correct!");
    }
}

The loop continues based on a condition rather than a predetermined number of repetitions.

docs.title: 8. Sentinel-Controlled Loops
docs.text:
Sometimes a program must process an unknown number of values.

A sentinel value is a special input value that signals the end of input.

Suppose 0 is used as the sentinel:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class SumValues {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        int sum = 0;

        System.out.print("Enter an integer (0 to stop): ");
        int number = input.nextInt();

        while (number != 0) {
            sum += number;

            System.out.print("Enter an integer (0 to stop): ");
            number = input.nextInt();
        }

        System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);
    }
}

The sentinel should normally be a value that is not intended to be processed as ordinary data.

docs.title: 9. Input Redirection
docs.text:
Programs that require large amounts of input can be inconvenient to test by manually entering every value.

One approach is to store test data in a file and redirect that file to the program's standard input from the command line.

Conceptually:

java ProgramName < input.txt

If the program reads from System.in, the values can be supplied from the file instead of typed one at a time.

This can make repeated testing with large datasets more efficient.

docs.title: 10. Avoid Floating-Point Equality for Loop Control
docs.text:
Floating-point numbers are represented approximately in a computer.

Therefore, a loop such as:

double value = 1.0;

while (value != 0.0) {
    value -= 0.1;
}

is risky. Repeated subtraction may not produce exactly 0.0.

A safer design is often to use an integer counter:

for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--) {
    double value = i / 10.0;
    System.out.println(value);
}

When possible, use integer-controlled iteration rather than relying on exact equality between repeatedly modified floating-point values.

docs.title: 11. The do-while Loop
docs.text:
General form:

do {
    // Loop body
} while (condition);

Unlike a while loop, a do-while loop checks its condition after executing the body.

Therefore, the body executes at least once.

Example:

int number = 1;

do {
    System.out.println(number);
    number++;
} while (number <= 5);

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

Notice the semicolon after:

while (condition);

It is required in a do-while statement.

docs.title: 12. When do-while Is Useful
docs.text:
A do-while loop is appropriate when an action should occur before deciding whether to repeat it.

A menu is a common example:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class MenuExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
        int choice;

        do {
            System.out.println("1. View Profile");
            System.out.println("2. Settings");
            System.out.println("0. Exit");
            System.out.print("Choice: ");

            choice = input.nextInt();

        } while (choice != 0);

        System.out.println("Program ended.");
    }
}

The menu appears at least once.

docs.title: 13. The for Loop
docs.text:
A for loop combines initialization, continuation condition, and update into one statement.

General form:

for (initialization; condition; update) {
    // Loop body
}

Example:

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

The execution sequence is:

Initialization
      ↓
Condition
      ↓ true
Loop body
      ↓
Update
      ↓
Condition again

The initialization executes only once.

docs.title: 14. Tracing a for Loop
docs.text:
Consider:

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Trace:

Step i Condition Action

Initialize 0 --- Set i to 0 Iteration 1 0 true Print 0 Update 1 --- i++ Iteration 2 1 true Print 1 Update 2 --- i++ Iteration 3 2 true Print 2 Update 3 --- i++ Exit 3 false Loop terminates

docs.title: 15. Counting Backward
docs.text:
A for loop can decrement instead of increment.

for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:

5
4
3
2
1

The update does not have to be i++. It can use another appropriate expression.

docs.title: 16. Changing the Step Size
docs.text:
A loop can change its counter by more than one.

Print even numbers from 2 through 10:

for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 2) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:

2
4
6
8
10

docs.title: 17. Multiple Expressions in a for Loop
docs.text:
The initialization and update portions of a for loop can contain multiple comma-separated expressions.

Example:

for (int left = 1, right = 10;
     left < right;
     left++, right--) {

    System.out.println(left + " " + right);
}

Although Java permits this form, simple loop headers are generally easier to read.

docs.title: 18. Choosing a Loop Structure
docs.text: The three loop structures can often be converted from one form to another, but one form may express the intent more clearly.

docs.title: Use a for loop when:
docs.text:
• The number of repetitions is known or naturally counter-controlled.
  • Initialization and update belong naturally in the loop header.

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    // Repeat 100 times
}

docs.title: Use a while loop when:
docs.text:
• The number of repetitions is not known in advance.
  • Repetition depends on input or another changing condition.

Example:

while (number != 0) {
    // Continue until sentinel
}

docs.title: Use a do-while loop when:
docs.text: • The body must execute at least once before the condition is tested.

docs.title: 19. Equivalent Loop Forms
docs.text:
This while loop:

int i = 0;

while (i < 5) {
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;
}

can be expressed as:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

The behavior is equivalent, but the for version groups the loop-control components together.

docs.title: 20. Nested Loops
docs.text:
A loop can appear inside another loop.

Example:

for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {

    for (int column = 1; column <= 4; column++) {
        System.out.print("* ");
    }

    System.out.println();
}

Output:

* * * *
* * * *
* * * *

For every one iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop executes all of its iterations.

docs.title: 21. Multiplication Table with Nested Loops
docs.text:
Nested loops are useful for tables.

for (int row = 1; row <= 5; row++) {

    for (int column = 1; column <= 5; column++) {
        System.out.printf("%4d", row * column);
    }

    System.out.println();
}

The outer loop controls the rows, while the inner loop controls the columns.

docs.title: 22. Understanding Nested Loop Counts
docs.text:
Consider:

for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {

    for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + ", " + j);
    }
}

The outer loop executes 4 times.

For each outer iteration, the inner loop executes 3 times.

Therefore, the println statement executes:

4 × 3 = 12 times

Understanding this multiplication effect is important when analyzing nested-loop performance.

docs.title: 23. Minimizing Numerical Errors
docs.text:
Repeated floating-point calculations can accumulate rounding errors.

For example, repeatedly adding 0.01 may not produce the exact mathematical value expected because many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point format.

When appropriate, perform repeated calculations using integer units and convert at the end.

Instead of relying on:

double amount = 0.0;

for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    amount += 0.01;
}

a program could represent cents as integers:

int cents = 0;

for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    cents += 1;
}

double dollars = cents / 100.0;

The best approach depends on the problem, but loop design should account for numerical precision.

docs.title: 24. Example: Greatest Common Divisor
docs.text:
Loops can solve mathematical search problems.

The following program finds the greatest common divisor of two positive integers by testing possible divisors:

int n1 = 24;
int n2 = 36;
int gcd = 1;

for (int k = 2; k <= n1 && k <= n2; k++) {

    if (n1 % k == 0 && n2 % k == 0) {
        gcd = k;
    }
}

System.out.println("GCD: " + gcd);

Output:

GCD: 12

The loop repeatedly tests candidate divisors and remembers the greatest one found.

docs.title: 25. Example: Repeated Growth
docs.text:
Loops are useful when a quantity changes repeatedly over time.

Suppose an amount begins at $10,000 and grows by 7% each year. The following loop determines how many years it takes to double:

double amount = 10000;
double target = amount * 2;
int years = 0;

while (amount < target) {
    amount *= 1.07;
    years++;
}

System.out.println("Years: " + years);
System.out.printf("Amount: $%.2f%n", amount);

This is a condition-controlled loop because the required number of years is determined during execution.

docs.title: 26. Example: Decimal to Hexadecimal Conversion
docs.text:
Repeated division can be used to convert a nonnegative decimal integer to hexadecimal.

int decimal = 254;
String hex = "";

do {
    int remainder = decimal % 16;

    char digit;

    if (remainder < 10) {
        digit = (char) ('0' + remainder);
    }
    else {
        digit = (char) ('A' + remainder - 10);
    }

    hex = digit + hex;
    decimal /= 16;

} while (decimal != 0);

System.out.println(hex);

Output:

FE

Each iteration obtains one hexadecimal digit from the remainder.

docs.title: 27. Simulation with Loops
docs.text:
Loops can repeat randomized experiments.

Example:

int heads = 0;
int tails = 0;

for (int trial = 0; trial < 1000; trial++) {

    if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
        heads++;
    }
    else {
        tails++;
    }
}

System.out.println("Heads: " + heads);
System.out.println("Tails: " + tails);

This illustrates the basic idea behind computational simulation: repeat an experiment many times and summarize the outcomes.

docs.title: 28. The break Statement
docs.text:
The break statement immediately terminates the nearest loop.

Example:

for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {

    if (i == 10) {
        break;
    }

    System.out.println(i);
}

When i becomes 10, the loop terminates.

The next statement after the loop executes.

docs.title: 29. The continue Statement
docs.text:
The continue statement skips the remainder of the current iteration and proceeds with the next iteration.

Example:

for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {

    if (i == 5) {
        continue;
    }

    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:

1
2
3
4
6
7
8
9
10

The value 5 is not printed.

docs.title: 30. break vs. continue
docs.text:
These statements have different effects:

Statement Effect

break Terminates the loop completely continue Skips the remainder of the current iteration

Use them carefully. Excessive use can make loop logic more difficult to follow.

docs.title: 31. Example: Palindrome Checking
docs.text:
A palindrome reads the same forward and backward.

Examples include:

level
radar
noon

A loop can compare characters from opposite ends of a string:

String text = "level";

int left = 0;
int right = text.length() - 1;
boolean palindrome = true;

while (left < right) {

    if (text.charAt(left) != text.charAt(right)) {
        palindrome = false;
        break;
    }

    left++;
    right--;
}

System.out.println("Palindrome: " + palindrome);

The loop stops when a mismatch is found or when all necessary character pairs have been checked.

docs.title: 32. Example: Testing for a Prime Number
docs.text:
A prime number is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.

int number = 29;
boolean prime = number > 1;

for (int divisor = 2;
     divisor <= Math.sqrt(number) && prime;
     divisor++) {

    if (number % divisor == 0) {
        prime = false;
    }
}

System.out.println("Prime: " + prime);

This demonstrates how loops and selection statements work together.

docs.title: 33. Common Error: Infinite Loops
docs.text:
An infinite loop never reaches a false continuation condition.

Example:

int count = 1;

while (count <= 10) {
    System.out.println(count);
}

The value of count never changes.

Correct version:

int count = 1;

while (count <= 10) {
    System.out.println(count);
    count++;
}

When a loop does not terminate as expected, check whether the variables used by its condition are being updated correctly.

docs.title: 34. Intentional Infinite Loops
docs.text:
Some programs intentionally create a loop that runs until an event causes it to stop.

Examples:

while (true) {
    // Repeat until a break or other termination mechanism
}

or:

for (;;) {
    // Infinite loop
}

Although both are legal Java, while (true) often communicates the intention more clearly.

docs.title: 35. Common Error: Semicolon After a Loop Header
docs.text:
Incorrect:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++);
{
    System.out.println("Java");
}

The semicolon terminates the for statement. The block is not the loop body.

Correct:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println("Java");
}

A similar mistake can occur with while.

Incorrect:

while (count < 5);
{
    count++;
}

Always inspect loop headers carefully when behavior does not match expectations.

docs.title: 36. Common Error: Off-by-One Errors
docs.text:
An off-by-one error occurs when a loop executes one time too many or one time too few.

Compare:

for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++)

with:

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)

The first executes for:

1, 2, 3, 4

The second executes for:

1, 2, 3, 4, 5

Pay close attention to:

  • Initial values
  • < versus <=
  • > versus >=
  • Increment and decrement operations

docs.title: 37. Variable Scope in Loops
docs.text:
A variable declared inside a for loop header is normally available only within that loop.

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

After the loop:

// System.out.println(i); // Error: i is out of scope

If the value is needed after the loop, declare it outside:

int i;

for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

System.out.println("Final i: " + i);

docs.title: 38. Debugging Loops
docs.text:
When a loop behaves incorrectly, examine its execution systematically.

Check:

  1. What is the initial value?
  2. What condition controls repetition?
  3. When is the condition evaluated?
  4. Which values change inside the loop?
  5. Does the update move the loop toward termination?
  6. How many iterations should occur?
  7. Are boundary values handled correctly?
  8. Is a semicolon accidentally terminating the loop header?
  9. Could break or continue alter the expected flow?
  10. Is floating-point equality being used as a stopping condition?

IDE debugging tools can also help by allowing you to set a breakpoint, execute one statement at a time, and inspect variable values after each iteration.

docs.title: 39. Loop Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Test loops with small inputs before using large values.

For example, instead of first testing:

for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)

temporarily test:

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)

This makes the execution easier to trace manually.

Also test boundary conditions.

For:

while (number <= 10)

consider values such as:

9
10
11

Boundary testing helps identify incorrect continuation conditions.

docs.title: 40. Putting the Concepts Together
docs.text:
The following program accepts an unknown number of positive scores, uses -1 as a sentinel, and calculates summary information.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class ScoreSummary {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        int count = 0;
        double total = 0;
        double highest = 0;

        System.out.print("Enter a score (-1 to finish): ");
        double score = input.nextDouble();

        while (score != -1) {

            if (score >= 0 && score <= 100) {

                total += score;
                count++;

                if (score > highest) {
                    highest = score;
                }
            }
            else {
                System.out.println("Invalid score.");
            }

            System.out.print("Enter a score (-1 to finish): ");
            score = input.nextDouble();
        }

        if (count > 0) {
            double average = total / count;

            System.out.println("Scores entered: " + count);
            System.out.printf("Average: %.2f%n", average);
            System.out.printf("Highest: %.2f%n", highest);
        }
        else {
            System.out.println("No valid scores were entered.");
        }
    }
}

This program combines:

  • A sentinel-controlled while loop
  • Input validation
  • A counter
  • An accumulator
  • Selection statements
  • Repeated input
  • Summary calculations

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. What are the four basic components commonly involved in loop design?
  2. What is an iteration?
  3. Why can a while loop execute zero times?
  4. What is the purpose of a loop counter?
  5. What is an accumulator?
  6. What is a sentinel value?
  7. When is a sentinel-controlled loop useful?
  8. What is the main difference between while and do-while?
  9. Why does a do-while loop execute at least once?
  10. What are the three components in a typical for loop header?
  11. When is a for loop generally preferable to a while loop?
  12. When is a while loop generally preferable to a for loop?
  13. What happens when one loop is nested inside another?
  14. Why should floating-point equality generally be avoided as a loop-continuation test?
  15. What does break do inside a loop?
  16. What does continue do inside a loop?
  17. What is an infinite loop?
  18. What can cause an off-by-one error?
  19. What happens if a semicolon is accidentally placed immediately after a for or while header?
  20. Why is tracing a loop with small input values useful for debugging?
  21. How can loops be used to solve search problems such as finding a greatest common divisor?
  22. How can a loop be used to determine whether a number is prime?

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As programs become larger, placing every statement inside main makes the code difficult to understand, test, and maintain. Methods allow a program to be divided into smaller units, where each unit performs a specific operation.

A well-designed method has a clear purpose, accepts only the information it needs, and may return a result to its caller. Methods also make it possible to reuse logic instead of rewriting the same code in several places.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this material, you should be able to:

  • Define and invoke Java methods.
  • Distinguish between formal parameters and arguments.
  • Identify a method's name, parameter list, return type, body, and signature.
  • Write methods that return values.
  • Write void methods that perform an action.
  • Explain how primitive values are passed to methods.
  • Use methods to reduce repeated code and organize a program into modules.
  • Overload methods appropriately.
  • Recognize ambiguous method calls.
  • Determine the scope of local variables.
  • Apply method abstraction to program design.
  • Decompose a larger problem into smaller methods using stepwise refinement.

docs.title: 1. Why Use Methods?
docs.text:
Suppose a program needs to calculate the sum of several different integer ranges. One approach is to repeat nearly identical loops:

int sum = 0;

for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    sum += i;
}

System.out.println(sum);

sum = 0;

for (int i = 20; i <= 30; i++) {
    sum += i;
}

System.out.println(sum);

The repeated logic can instead be placed in a method:

public static int sumRange(int start, int end) {
    int sum = 0;

    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        sum += i;
    }

    return sum;
}

The method can then be reused:

System.out.println(sumRange(1, 10));
System.out.println(sumRange(20, 30));
System.out.println(sumRange(35, 45));

The program becomes shorter and the purpose of the repeated operation becomes clearer.

docs.title: 2. What Is a Method?
docs.text:
A method is a named group of statements designed to perform an operation.

Example:

public static int larger(int first, int second) {

    if (first > second) {
        return first;
    }

    return second;
}

This method receives two integers and returns the larger value.

A method normally contains several important components:

modifier  return type  method name  parameter list
   ↓           ↓            ↓            ↓
public static int        larger(int first, int second)

The statements inside the braces form the method body.

docs.title: 3. Method Header and Method Body
docs.text:
Consider:

public static double calculateArea(double radius) {
    double area = Math.PI * radius * radius;
    return area;
}

The header is:

public static double calculateArea(double radius)

It identifies:

  • Modifiers: public static
  • Return type: double
  • Method name: calculateArea
  • Parameter: double radius

The body is:

{
    double area = Math.PI * radius * radius;
    return area;
}

The body contains the implementation of the operation.

docs.title: 4. Method Signature
docs.text:
A method's signature consists of:

method name + parameter list

For example:

public static int multiply(int a, int b)

has the signature:

multiply(int, int)

The return type is not part of the method signature.

This becomes especially important when working with overloaded methods.

docs.title: 5. Formal Parameters
docs.text:
Variables declared in a method's parameter list are called formal parameters.

public static int subtract(int first, int second) {
    return first - second;
}

Here:

first
second

are formal parameters.

They receive values when the method is invoked.

docs.title: 6. Arguments
docs.text:
Values supplied when a method is invoked are called arguments.

int result = subtract(20, 8);

Here:

20
8

are arguments.

They correspond to:

first = 20
second = 8

The arguments must be compatible with the method's parameter types and must appear in the correct order.

docs.title: 7. Defining and Invoking a Method
docs.text:
A method definition describes what the method does.

public static int square(int number) {
    return number * number;
}

A method invocation requests that operation:

int answer = square(7);

Execution temporarily transfers to square. After the method finishes, its return value is assigned to answer.

main
  |
  | square(7)
  v
square
  |
  | return 49
  v
main

docs.title: 8. Value-Returning Methods
docs.text:
A value-returning method sends a result back to its caller.

Example:

public static double convertMilesToKilometers(double miles) {
    return miles * 1.60934;
}

Invocation:

double km = convertMilesToKilometers(10);

The method's declared return type must be compatible with the value returned.

docs.title: 9. The return Statement
docs.text:
The return statement ends a method and sends a value back to the caller.

public static int cube(int number) {
    return number * number * number;
}

For a value-returning method, every possible execution path must return an appropriate value.

A problematic method might be:

public static int absoluteValue(int number) {

    if (number < 0) {
        return -number;
    }
}

If number is not negative, no value is returned.

A correct version is:

public static int absoluteValue(int number) {

    if (number < 0) {
        return -number;
    }

    return number;
}

docs.title: 10. Using a Returned Value
docs.text: A returned value can be:

docs.title: Assigned to a variable
docs.text: double area = calculateArea(5);

docs.title: Printed directly
docs.text: System.out.println(calculateArea(5));

docs.title: Used in an expression
docs.text: double totalArea = calculateArea(5) + calculateArea(3);

docs.title: Passed to another method
docs.text:
System.out.println(Math.round(calculateArea(5)));

This flexibility makes value-returning methods useful building blocks.

docs.title: 11. void Methods
docs.text:
A method that does not return a value uses the return type void.

public static void displayWelcome() {
    System.out.println("Welcome to Java");
}

Invoke it with:

displayWelcome();

A void method performs an action rather than producing a value for use in an expression.

docs.title: 12. void Methods with Parameters
docs.text:
A void method can still receive information.

public static void printMessage(String message, int times) {

    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) {
        System.out.println(message);
    }
}

Invocation:

printMessage("Java Methods", 3);

Output:

Java Methods
Java Methods
Java Methods

The order of the arguments matters because they correspond to the parameters by position.

docs.title: 13. Returning Early from a void Method
docs.text:
A void method can use:

return;

to terminate early.

Example:

public static void printPositive(int number) {

    if (number <= 0) {
        return;
    }

    System.out.println(number);
}

No value follows return because the method's return type is void.

docs.title: 14. Parameter Type and Order
docs.text:
Suppose a method is defined as:

public static void repeat(String message, int count) {
    // ...
}

This invocation is valid:

repeat("Hello", 5);

This is not:

// repeat(5, "Hello");

The compiler compares the arguments with the method's parameter list.

Correct order and compatible data types are required.

docs.title: 15. Pass by Value
docs.text:
Java passes argument values to method parameters.

For primitive types, the method receives a copy of the value.

Consider:

public static void changeValue(int number) {
    number = 100;
}

and:

int x = 10;

changeValue(x);

System.out.println(x);

Output:

10

Changing number does not change x.

Conceptually:

x in main:       10
                  |
                  | copy value
                  v
number in method: 10

number = 100

x in main:       10
number in method:100

The two variables are separate.

docs.title: 16. Why a Primitive Swap Method Does Not Swap the Caller
docs.text:
Consider:

public static void swap(int first, int second) {

    int temp = first;
    first = second;
    second = temp;
}

Now:

int x = 4;
int y = 9;

swap(x, y);

System.out.println(x + " " + y);

Output:

4 9

Inside swap, the copies are exchanged. The original variables in the caller remain unchanged.

docs.title: 17. Method Calls and the Call Stack
docs.text:
Each active method call needs its own execution information, including parameters and local variables.

Suppose:

public static void main(String[] args) {

    int x = 8;
    int y = 3;

    int result = larger(x, y);

    System.out.println(result);
}

When larger(x, y) is invoked, the caller pauses while the called method executes.

Conceptually:

larger
----------------
first = 8
second = 3

main
----------------
x = 8
y = 3
result = ?

After larger returns, its method-call information is removed and execution continues in main.

Understanding this process helps explain why local variables in separate method calls are independent.

docs.title: 18. Reusing Methods from Another Class
docs.text:
A reusable static method can be called from another class by qualifying the method name with the class name.

Suppose:

public class NumberTools {

    public static int larger(int a, int b) {
        return a > b ? a : b;
    }
}

Another class can call:

int result = NumberTools.larger(12, 7);

This allows related reusable operations to be organized into utility classes.

docs.title: 19. Modularizing a Program
docs.text:
Methods can divide a larger problem into smaller responsibilities.

Instead of:

public static void main(String[] args) {
    // read data
    // validate data
    // calculate results
    // determine status
    // print report
}

use:

public static void main(String[] args) {

    double score = readScore();
    boolean valid = isValidScore(score);

    if (valid) {
        String grade = determineGrade(score);
        printReport(score, grade);
    }
}

Each method represents one meaningful operation.

This makes the program easier to read, test, debug, and modify.

docs.title: 20. Example: Greatest Common Divisor Method
docs.text:
A mathematical operation can be encapsulated in a reusable method.

public static int gcd(int first, int second) {

    int gcd = 1;

    for (int divisor = 1;
         divisor <= first && divisor <= second;
         divisor++) {

        if (first % divisor == 0 &&
            second % divisor == 0) {

            gcd = divisor;
        }
    }

    return gcd;
}

Invocation:

System.out.println(gcd(24, 36));

Output:

12

The caller does not need to know how the divisor search is implemented.

docs.title: 21. Example: Prime Number Method
docs.text:
A method can answer a focused yes/no question by returning a boolean.

public static boolean isPrime(int number) {

    if (number < 2) {
        return false;
    }

    for (int divisor = 2;
         divisor <= Math.sqrt(number);
         divisor++) {

        if (number % divisor == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    return true;
}

Usage:

if (isPrime(29)) {
    System.out.println("29 is prime.");
}

The method name makes the condition easy to understand.

docs.title: 22. Example: Hexadecimal Digit Conversion
docs.text:
Methods can separate a conversion problem into smaller operations.

For example, one method can convert a hexadecimal digit to its decimal value:

public static int hexDigitToDecimal(char digit) {

    if (digit >= '0' && digit <= '9') {
        return digit - '0';
    }

    if (digit >= 'A' && digit <= 'F') {
        return digit - 'A' + 10;
    }

    return -1;
}

Another method can use it repeatedly:

public static int hexToDecimal(String hex) {

    int decimal = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < hex.length(); i++) {

        int value = hexDigitToDecimal(
            Character.toUpperCase(hex.charAt(i))
        );

        if (value == -1) {
            return -1;
        }

        decimal = decimal * 16 + value;
    }

    return decimal;
}

This illustrates decomposition: one method solves the digit-level problem while another solves the complete conversion.

docs.title: 23. Method Overloading
docs.text:
Java permits multiple methods to have the same name when their parameter lists are different.

Example:

public static int larger(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

public static double larger(double a, double b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

Now:

larger(4, 7);

uses the int version, while:

larger(4.5, 7.2);

uses the double version.

This is called method overloading.

docs.title: 24. What Makes Overloaded Methods Different?
docs.text:
Overloaded methods must have different parameter lists.

Differences may involve:

  • Number of parameters
  • Parameter data types
  • Order of parameter types

Example:

public static void display(int value) { }

public static void display(double value) { }

public static void display(String value) { }

public static void display(String text, int count) { }

Changing only the return type is not sufficient.

This is invalid:

// public static int calculate(int x) { ... }
// public static double calculate(int x) { ... }

Both methods would have the same signature.

docs.title: 25. Ambiguous Method Invocation
docs.text:
Overloading must be designed carefully.

Suppose:

public static double calculate(int x, double y) {
    return x + y;
}

public static double calculate(double x, int y) {
    return x + y;
}

A call such as:

// calculate(5, 5);

can be ambiguous because either overloaded version appears applicable through numeric conversion.

If the compiler cannot determine the most specific method, compilation fails.

docs.title: 26. Local Variables
docs.text:
A variable declared inside a method is a local variable.

public static double calculateTax(double amount) {

    double taxRate = 0.08;
    double tax = amount * taxRate;

    return tax;
}

Here:

amount
taxRate
tax

are available only within the region where their declarations are in scope.

docs.title: 27. Variable Scope
docs.text:
Scope is the portion of a program in which a variable can be referenced.

Example:

public static void example() {

    int x = 10;

    if (x > 0) {
        int y = 20;

        System.out.println(x);
        System.out.println(y);
    }

    System.out.println(x);

    // System.out.println(y); // Error
}

x is available through the method block after its declaration.

y exists only inside the if block.

docs.title: 28. Scope in for Loops
docs.text:
A variable declared in the initialization section of a for loop belongs to that loop.

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

// i cannot be referenced here

Two separate, non-nested loops can each declare their own i:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    // ...
}

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    // ...
}

The scopes do not overlap.

docs.title: 29. Avoid Redeclaring Variables in Nested Scope
docs.text:
Consider:

public static void example() {

    int value = 10;

    if (value > 0) {
        // int value = 20; // Not allowed
    }
}

The inner block is nested within the scope of the existing local variable.

Choose distinct names instead:

int value = 10;

if (value > 0) {
    int adjustedValue = 20;
}

docs.title: 30. Method Abstraction
docs.text:
A caller should be able to use a method based on its purpose and interface without needing to understand every implementation detail.

For example:

double distance = calculateDistance(x1, y1, x2, y2);

The caller needs to know:

  • What the method does
  • What arguments it requires
  • What it returns

The detailed formula can remain inside the method.

This is method abstraction.

You can think of the method as a black box:

        input
          |
          v
+--------------------+
| calculateDistance  |
| implementation     |
| hidden inside      |
+--------------------+
          |
          v
        result

docs.title: 31. Benefits of Method Abstraction
docs.text:
Method abstraction helps a programmer:

  • Reuse operations.
  • Hide implementation details.
  • Reduce complexity.
  • Focus on one level of a problem at a time.
  • Test individual operations independently.
  • Change an implementation without rewriting every caller.

A descriptive method name also makes code more self-explanatory.

docs.title: 32. Example: Random Character Method
docs.text:
A general-purpose method can generate a random character between two character values:

public static char randomCharacter(char first, char last) {

    return (char) (
        first +
        Math.random() * (last - first + 1)
    );
}

Specialized methods can reuse it:

public static char randomLowercaseLetter() {
    return randomCharacter('a', 'z');
}

public static char randomUppercaseLetter() {
    return randomCharacter('A', 'Z');
}

public static char randomDigit() {
    return randomCharacter('0', '9');
}

This design places the general calculation in one reusable method and gives meaningful names to common specialized operations.

docs.title: 33. Stepwise Refinement
docs.text:
Large programming problems are easier to manage when divided into smaller problems.

This process is often called stepwise refinement or divide and conquer.

Suppose the task is:

Produce a monthly calendar

A first decomposition might be:

produceCalendar
├── readInput
└── printMonth

Then:

printMonth
├── printMonthTitle
└── printMonthBody

The smaller operations can be refined further:

printMonthTitle
└── getMonthName

printMonthBody
├── getStartDay
└── getNumberOfDaysInMonth

Eventually, each method represents a manageable task.

docs.title: 34. Structure Charts
docs.text:
A structure chart can show the relationship among methods before implementation begins.

Example:

main
├── readInput
├── validateInput
├── calculateResult
│   ├── calculateSubtotal
│   └── calculateAdjustment
└── displayReport

This helps identify:

  • Major tasks
  • Subtasks
  • Method responsibilities
  • Opportunities for reuse
  • Dependencies between operations

Designing the method structure before coding can simplify implementation.

docs.title: 35. Top-Down Development
docs.text:
A top-down approach begins with the highest-level method and works toward lower-level details.

A programmer might first write:

public static void main(String[] args) {

    readInput();
    processData();
    displayResults();
}

The detailed methods can initially be represented by stubs.

Example:

public static void processData() {
    System.out.println("processData called");
}

The stub is intentionally incomplete but allows the program's overall structure to be compiled and tested while development continues.

docs.title: 36. Bottom-Up Development
docs.text:
A bottom-up approach begins with smaller supporting methods.

For example, a programmer may implement and test:

isValidDate
isLeapYear
daysInMonth

before implementing a larger method that depends on them.

Each method can be tested independently before being integrated into the larger program.

Both top-down and bottom-up approaches can be useful, and a project may combine them.

docs.title: 37. Designing Good Methods
docs.text:
A useful method should normally perform one clear task.

Prefer:

public static boolean isValidScore(double score)

public static double calculateAverage(double total, int count)

public static void displayReport(double average)

over one very large method containing unrelated responsibilities.

Good method names should communicate intent.

Prefer:

calculateTuition()

instead of:

doStuff()

docs.title: 38. Methods and Repeated Logic
docs.text:
Repeated code often indicates an opportunity for a method.

Instead of:

double area1 = Math.PI * 4 * 4;
double area2 = Math.PI * 8 * 8;
double area3 = Math.PI * 12 * 12;

write:

public static double circleArea(double radius) {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
}

Then:

double area1 = circleArea(4);
double area2 = circleArea(8);
double area3 = circleArea(12);

If the formula changes, only one implementation needs to be updated.

docs.title: 39. Common Error: Forgetting to Return a Value
docs.text:
Incorrect:

public static int larger(int a, int b) {

    if (a > b) {
        return a;
    }
}

There is no return value when a <= b.

Correct:

public static int larger(int a, int b) {

    if (a > b) {
        return a;
    }
    else {
        return b;
    }
}

docs.title: 40. Common Error: Incorrect Argument Order
docs.text:
Suppose:

public static double divide(double numerator,
                            double denominator) {
    return numerator / denominator;
}

These calls produce different results:

divide(10, 2);
divide(2, 10);

Arguments are matched to parameters by position.

docs.title: 41. Common Error: Expecting Primitive Arguments to Change
docs.text:
Incorrect assumption:

public static void doubleValue(int value) {
    value *= 2;
}

Calling:

int number = 5;
doubleValue(number);

does not change number.

If the transformed value is needed, return it:

public static int doubleValue(int value) {
    return value * 2;
}

Then:

number = doubleValue(number);

docs.title: 42. Common Error: Confusing void and Value-Returning Methods
docs.text:
A void method cannot be used as though it produces a value.

Given:

public static void displayMessage() {
    System.out.println("Hello");
}

this is invalid:

// String message = displayMessage();

If a result is needed, define a value-returning method instead.

docs.title: 43. Common Error: Scope Violations
docs.text:
Incorrect:

if (true) {
    int score = 90;
}

System.out.println(score);

score is no longer in scope outside the block.

Declare the variable in a wider scope when it must be used later:

int score;

if (true) {
    score = 90;
}

System.out.println(score);

docs.title: 44. Testing Methods Independently
docs.text:
Small methods are easier to test than one large program.

Suppose:

public static boolean isEven(int number) {
    return number % 2 == 0;
}

Test several categories:

System.out.println(isEven(4));   // true
System.out.println(isEven(7));   // false
System.out.println(isEven(0));   // true
System.out.println(isEven(-2));  // true

Testing boundary and unusual values can reveal errors before the method is integrated into a larger application.

docs.title: 45. Putting the Concepts Together
docs.text:
The following example separates a simple student-result application into focused methods.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class StudentResult {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter score: ");
        double score = input.nextDouble();

        if (isValidScore(score)) {

            char grade = determineGrade(score);
            displayResult(score, grade);

        }
        else {
            System.out.println("Invalid score.");
        }
    }

    public static boolean isValidScore(double score) {
        return score >= 0 && score <= 100;
    }

    public static char determineGrade(double score) {

        if (score >= 90)
            return 'A';
        else if (score >= 80)
            return 'B';
        else if (score >= 70)
            return 'C';
        else if (score >= 60)
            return 'D';
        else
            return 'F';
    }

    public static void displayResult(double score, char grade) {

        System.out.printf(
            "Score: %.1f%nGrade: %c%n",
            score,
            grade
        );
    }
}

This program demonstrates:

  • Method definitions
  • Method invocation
  • Formal parameters
  • Arguments
  • boolean return values
  • char return values
  • A void method
  • Method abstraction
  • Modular program organization
